lessonInput.title: Electric current
lessonInput.objectives: Use only the supplied claims to make a defensible distinction without adding outside facts.
lessonInput.topics: Claim 0: Electric current is the rate at which charge passes through a surface. Claim 1: Conventional current direction is the direction positive charge would move. Claim 2: Microscopic drift speed is slow even though the electric signal through a circuit propagates rapidly.

keyTerms.df: Electric current is a rate quantity defined by charge passing through a surface.
keyTerms.eg: Charge passes through a surface, and electric current reports the associated rate.
keyTerms.mi: Electric current names the surface through which charge passes.
keyTerms.cx: The surface marks where passage occurs; current describes the rate of that passage.

keyTerms.df: Conventional current direction identifies the direction in which positive charge would move.
keyTerms.eg: Positive charge would move in the conventional current direction.
keyTerms.mi: Conventional current direction is the rate at which positive charge passes.
keyTerms.cx: It specifies possible positive-charge motion in a direction rather than measuring passage rate.

keyTerms.df: Microscopic drift speed is slow compared with the rapidly propagating electric signal through a circuit.
keyTerms.eg: A circuit comparison pairs slow microscopic drift speed with rapid electric-signal propagation.
keyTerms.mi: Microscopic drift speed propagates rapidly while the electric signal is slow.
keyTerms.cx: The rapid propagation belongs to the electric signal, while microscopic drift remains slow.

scenario.su: A workshop group must assign accurate labels to four statements about charge, direction, drift speed, and signal propagation. The group faces a deadline and must distinguish the paired ideas using the stated observations rather than treating their properties as interchangeable.
scenario.ma: charge-through-surface rate notation, positive-charge direction notation, slow-drift observation, rapid-signal observation

mc.q: A comparison records charge passing through a surface at a rate and separately marks the direction positive charge would move. Which distinction correctly labels electric current and conventional current direction?
op: Current gives charge-passage rate; conventional direction tracks positive charge
Current tracks positive charge; conventional direction gives passage rate
Current gives positive-charge direction; conventional direction marks surface
Current marks the surface; conventional direction gives charge rate
mc.ex: Electric current is the rate of charge passing through a surface, whereas conventional current direction follows the direction positive charge would move. The two relations should not be exchanged between rate and direction.

mc.q: In a circuit comparison, the recorded microscopic drift speed is slow while the observed electric signal propagates rapidly. Under a constraint requiring one accurate paired label, which notation is supported?
op: Drift speed is slow; electric signal propagates rapidly
Drift speed is rapid; electric signal propagates slowly
Drift speed is rapid; electric signal propagates rapidly
Drift speed is slow; electric signal propagates slowly
mc.ex: Microscopic drift speed is slow even though the electric signal through a circuit propagates rapidly. Rapid propagation therefore describes the signal, not the microscopic drift speed.
